OpenRFM: Dissecting Relational In-Context Learning

Zhikai Chen Junyu Yin11footnotemark: 1  Jialiang Gu11footnotemark: 1  Siheng Xiong ††thanks: Equal contribution. Affiliation: Michigan State University Affiliation: Georgia Institute of Technology Affiliation: George Mason University    Xiaoze Liu Affiliation: Purdue University    Ruowang Zhang Affiliation: Purdue University    Keren Zhou Affiliation: George Mason University    Kai Guo ††thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: Michigan State University
Abstract

Relational Foundation Models (RFMs) promise a single pre-trained predictor that, given any relational database, returns predictions in one forward pass via relational in-context learning (ICL). Yet a substantial gap separates open RFMs from their commercial counterparts, and the origin of this gap has not been systematically understood. We dissect a representative framework, the Relational Transformer (RT), from two perspectives. Model side: we show that RT performs relation-level ICL, and a kernel regression view shows it fails when sparse label-cell coverage yields an underdetermined regression. Data side: we ablate RT’s pre-training source and find that existing synthetic-only pre-training and in-distribution pre-training drive the same architecture into different regimes, lazy vs. feature-learning. Probing this gap reveals that the missing ingredient is a support-identifiable relational latent in the label-generation process. These two diagnoses translate into (1) a dual-stage ICL architecture that combines the relational backbone with a batch-level ICL layer lifted from a pre-trained tabular foundation model to overcome relation-level label scarcity, and (2) a homophily-aware synthetic plus continual real-data pre-training mixture, augmented with a prototype-based regularization. These choices define OpenRFM, a simple yet effective RFM that improves average task performance by approximately 30%30\% over the RT backbone and surpasses the commercial model KumoRFMv1 on a large set of evaluation tasks.

1 Introduction

Relational databases [11] remain the dominant paradigm for storing enterprise data, underpinning applications from healthcare [27] and recommendations [37] to fraud detection [24]. These data systems carry two levels of structure: inner-table relations captured by the schema of individual tables and cross-table relations through primary key–foreign key references. Predictive modeling over such data has traditionally required task-specific models (e.g., XGBoost [5]) fed by hand-crafted feature joins and hyperparameter tuning, a pipeline that is labor-intensive and difficult to scale.

Relational Foundation Models (RFMs) [16, 55] address this overhead by pre-training a generalist predictor over a prior of diverse relational data, amortizing inference into one model that applies across domains. Once pre-trained, an RFM can produce predictions for a new task in a single forward pass through relational in-context learning (ICL). Recent results show that well-trained RFMs can match or surpass well-tuned task-specific models [16].

However, promising RFMs today are commercial [16, 23], and the only competitive open alternative depends on per-task and CPU-bound feature composition [55]. The cause of this gap remains poorly understood, so principled choices for backbone design and pre-training are still out of reach. For open parametric models, the Relational Transformer (RT) [40] offers a general framework for relational ICL, yet it still collapses on many downstream tasks. The pre-training recipe sits in a similar place: PluRel [32] adapts TabPFN’s prior-fitting paradigm [22] to relational data via synthetic databases, sidestepping the scarcity of real relational pre-training data; yet neither purely synthetic nor real-world pre-training delivers satisfactory downstream performance without task-specific continual training.

To demystify these gaps, we analyze both model and data design, from empirical observation down to mechanistic explanation. (1) Model side. We first observe that RT’s failure modes correlate strongly with how many label-carrying cells (the “C” in the unrolled sequence of Figure 1) land in the sampled context. Building on this signal, we show that RT is performing relation-level ICL: the label-carrying cells gathered along the BFS walk form the support set of an implicit kernel regression, and sparse label-cell coverage therefore yields an underdetermined regression. (2) Data side. Ablating RT’s pre-training source, we find that synthetic-only and real-world in-distribution training drive the same architecture into qualitatively different regimes: a near-fixed, lazy kernel under PluRel [32] synthetic, and a feature-learning regime [8] when pre-training on in-distribution tasks. Probing this gap reveals that the missing ingredient of existing synthetic pre-training is the modeling of latent relational diversity during the causal label-generation process: only when each pre-training episode is parameterized by a support-identifiable relational latent, which we realize through relational homophily [7], does RT cross out of the lazy regime.

Each diagnosis points to a concrete design change in the parametric RFM pipeline. (D1) Backbone: dual-stage in-context learning. The label-scarcity bottleneck identified on the model side is, structurally, a limitation of relying only on relation-level context construction. We therefore introduce dual-stage ICL: relation-level RT blocks are combined with a complementary batch-level ICL layer extracted from a pre-trained tabular foundation model (TFM), so that each query can attend both to its FK neighborhood and to all support rows in the batch. (D2) Pre-training: homophily-aware synthetic plus continual real data. On the data side, we augment PluRel-style synthetic generation with a homophily-aware diverse corpus, then mix this synthetic pre-training with continual pre-training on real-world databases. We further add a prototype-based regularization to stabilize multi-class readout under varying class-representation geometry. Together, these components define OpenRFM, a simple yet effective recipe for parametric RFMs that improves average task performance by approximately 30%30\% over the RT backbone with more task types supported, and surpasses KumoRFMv1 on a large set of evaluation tasks.

2 Preliminaries

2.1 Problem Setup and Relational Foundation Models

Problem background. We follow the relational deep learning (RDL) framework [15, 42], in which an RDB is paired with a task table whose rows specify target entities, timestamps, and labels; rows are gathered by a query language [42, 31] that traverses the RDB as of each row’s timestamp. We evaluate on temporal predictive tasks (e.g., customer churn) and autocomplete tasks (inferring missing attributes from relational evidence).

Relational foundation models. A relational foundation model (RFM) is a single pre-trained model fθf_{\theta} that, given an unseen RDB 𝒟\mathcal{D} and a task table 𝒯\mathcal{T} specifying a small set of in-context (support) rows 𝒮⊂𝒯\mathcal{S}\subset\mathcal{T} with labels and a query row x⋆∈𝒯x_{\star}\in\mathcal{T}, produces a prediction y^⋆=fθ​(x⋆∣𝒮,𝒟)\hat{y}_{\star}=f_{\theta}(x_{\star}\mid\mathcal{S},\mathcal{D}) in a single forward pass without any gradient update [16]. The criterion is inductive generalization: θ\theta is learned from a distribution of pre-training databases and tasks, yet must transfer to RDBs with unseen schemas, column semantics, and label spaces at test time.

RFM in-context learning design. Nonparametric approaches (DFS [28], Juice [55]) chain fixed aggregation primitives (MEAN, COUNT, MAX) along foreign-key paths to materialize features, then feed them to a tabular foundation model (TFM) at inference. For parametric counterparts, The standard RDL pipeline—a row-level GNN producing one row-level embedding per entity, fed to a task head—is structurally mis-specified for ICL [55]. Parametric RFMs therefore turn to cell-level designs, attending to cell-level tokens and jointly encoding the query with its in-context support; the Relational Transformer (RT) [40], detailed in Section 2.2, instantiates this design and serves as our representative throughout the paper.

RFM pre-training design. Existing RFMs differ on what to pre-train on and how much downstream adaptation they require. Griffin [47] pre-trains only the feature encoder, leaving the GNN to be fine-tuned per database with task-specific data and tuning. RT [40] pre-trains end-to-end on a curated set of real-database tasks, but strong numbers still require per-task checkpoint selection. To shed dependence on benchmark task tables, RDB-PFN [48] and PluRel [32] switch to synthetic pre-training data: RDB-PFN fits a PFN-style backbone on DFS-aggregated synthetic features, while PluRel generates native synthetic RDBs and trains RT on them (prior fitting and synthetic-data design are detailed in Section 3.2). TVE [44] replaces task supervision with a batch-statistics objective, which captures one-hop signal but does not scale to deeper neighborhoods. We refer to RT trained only on PluRel synthetic data as RT-synthetic and RT trained across all RelBench-v1 tasks as RT-cotrain; the gap between them motivates Section 3, and Table 1 summarizes where each RFM sits on these axes.

2.2 The Relational Transformer

Relational Transformer. Given a target entity e⋆e_{\star} at prediction time t⋆t_{\star}, RT [40] unrolls the temporally-valid BFS neighborhood of e⋆e_{\star} into a length-LL sequence of cell tokens, which are encoded by type-aware encoders. A set of schema-aware sparse masks ℳ={𝐌col,𝐌row,𝐌fk,𝐌full}\mathcal{M}=\{\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{col}},\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{row}},\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{fk}},\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{full}}\} (column, intra-row, FK-neighbour, full) is applied as sequential masked-attention residuals within each block, followed by a feed-forward residual,

𝐙0=𝐗(ℓ),𝐙k\displaystyle\mathbf{Z}_{0}=\mathbf{X}^{(\ell)},\quad\mathbf{Z}_{k} =𝐙k−1+Attn(Norm(𝐙k−1);𝐌k),𝐌k∈ℳ,\displaystyle=\mathbf{Z}_{k-1}+\mathrm{Attn}\!\big(\mathrm{Norm}(\mathbf{Z}_{k-1});\,\mathbf{M}_{k}\big),\quad\mathbf{M}_{k}\in\mathcal{M}, (1)
𝐗(ℓ+1)\displaystyle\mathbf{X}^{(\ell+1)} =𝐙|ℳ|+FFN⁡(Normffn​(𝐙|ℳ|)).\displaystyle=\mathbf{Z}_{|\mathcal{M}|}+\mathrm{FFN}\!\big(\mathrm{Norm}_{\mathrm{ffn}}(\mathbf{Z}_{|\mathcal{M}|})\big).

𝐗(M)\mathbf{X}^{(M)} is the output of the final (MM-th) block and 𝐗⋆(M)\mathbf{X}^{(M)}_{\star} is its target-cell row. Compared to row-level models like GNNs, RT realises the cross-table attention that Hudovernik et al. [23] identifies as the essential mechanism for relational ICL.

Pre-training and inference. RT is pre-trained by masking the label cell Y⋆Y_{\star} at the target position in the unrolled context (the YY slot in Figure 1) and predicting it from the remaining tokens. At inference, the readout at the target position emits y^⋆\hat{y}_{\star} in a single forward pass. Pre-training data can be real-world (a curated set of RDBs with their task tables) or synthetic [32], where schemas, foreign-key edges, per-column feature distributions, and a label column are sampled per episode through a structural causal model. Appendix E describes the design of PluRel in more details.

3 Diagnosing Relational In-Context Learning

3.1 Examining the RFM Backbone

We begin with revisiting RT’s performance on the popular RelBench-v1 tasks. We compare it to representative baselines including traditional tabular models [30], GNN training from scratch [42], and a non-parametric relational ICL method, JUICE [55]. We defer full per-task numbers to Appendix C and surface in the main text only differentiating tasks (Table 3), those on which different methods separate by a non-trivial margin.

The key failure mode is that RT underperforms on st-outc and st-adv, trailing even LightGBM, a baseline that discards relational context entirely. Recall (§2.2) that RT’s relational signal arrives only when its BFS walk reaches another row of the task table, whose label becomes part of the context. The effectiveness of this mechanism therefore depends on whether such labelled rows are reachable within the walk. For a task table 𝒯\mathcal{T} and seeds 𝒮\mathcal{S}, define ρ(𝒯)=|𝒮|−1∑s∈𝒮𝟏[∃v∈walk(s)∖{s}:v∈𝒯]\rho(\mathcal{T})=|\mathcal{S}|^{-1}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\mathbf{1}[\exists\,v\in\mathrm{walk}(s)\setminus\{s\}:v\in\mathcal{T}], where walk⁡(s)\mathrm{walk}(s) is the set of nodes visited by the relational BFS walk from ss (for autocomplete tasks the walk starts from the entity table on which the target column lives). RT excels on high-ρ\rho tasks and collapses on low-ρ\rho ones (Table 3; demonstrated with RT-synthetic, the pattern persists across pre-training regimes).

3.1.1 Understanding the Mechanism of RT’s ICL

To probe why RT fails, we run a context-corruption experiment [50] with two augmentations on the walked rows (excluding the seed): (1) shuffle label: permute label values across neighbours; (2) random features: permute non-label columns across neighbours. We compare two pre-training regimes: synthetic-only on PluRel and in-distribution, i.e. joint training on all evaluation tasks [40]. In-distribution training acts as an upper bound: it leaks task-specific signal at training time and breaks the strict relational-ICL setting.

Table 2 reveals a qualitative split between the pre-training regimes, which we read off as two insights. (I1) RT admits a kernel-regression-like label-transfer view. RT’s target-cell readout is computed by attention over the unrolled context sequence, and the labeled cells in that sequence are exactly the support 𝒮\mathcal{S} of reachable rows. If we abstract the multi-layer backbone into a feature map ϕ⁡(⋅)\boldsymbol{\phi}(\cdot) on rows and isolate the contribution of the final query-to-support attention head that writes into the target cell, then – linearising over residual / feed-forward branches and assuming the readout is dominated by that head – the prediction takes the kernel-regression-like form y^⋆≈∑i∈𝒮α⁡(x⋆,xi)​yi\hat{y}_{\star}\approx\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}\alpha(x_{\star},x_{i})\,y_{i} with α\alpha given by softmax attention over ϕ\boldsymbol{\phi}. This is the regime under which transformer attention has been connected to ridge / kernel-regression predictors [1, 45, 19]. This lens explains Section 3.1: reading the label reachability ρ\rho as the density of available regression targets, low-ρ\rho tasks correspond to a near-empty support, and the regression becomes ill-posed. (I2) The pre-training source determines whether ϕ\boldsymbol{\phi} is frozen or learned. Under PluRel synthetic pre-training, both shuffling labels and randomizing non-label features yield near-inconsequential drops, the signature of a lazy, frozen-feature regime [25, 8] in which ϕ\boldsymbol{\phi} is held fixed and the support is read only through its Gram matrix, collapsing the solution toward the mean support label y¯𝒮\bar{y}_{\mathcal{S}}. Under in-distribution pre-training, both invariances break and downstream metrics improve uniformly: this suggests the feature-learning regime [56] where ϕ\boldsymbol{\phi} co-adapts with labels.

3.2 Examining RFM Pre-training

The corruption probe of §3.1.1 delivers an empirical fact: the same RT crosses between a lazy, kernel-machine regime and a feature-learning regime depending only on the pre-training corpus. The natural question is therefore which property of the pre-training prior is causally responsible for the regime that the population-optimal predictor lives in.

Pre-training through posterior-predictive prior fitting.

Prior fitting [34, 35, 22] has been brought to relational data by RDB-PFN [48] and PluRel [32]: a prior-fitted network drawn from a pre-training prior Π\Pi over (database, task) pairs approximates the Bayesian posterior predictive

q⋆​(y⋆∣x⋆,D)=∫p⁡(y⋆∣x⋆,z)​p​(z∣D)​𝑑z,D={(xi,yi)}i=1n,q^{\star}(y^{\star}\mid x^{\star},D)\;=\;\int p(y^{\star}\mid x^{\star},z)\,p(z\mid D)\,dz,\qquad D=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}, (2)

where zz is the per-episode data-generating mechanism. Under the standard ICL assumption that y⋆⟂YS|z,x⋆,XSy^{\star}\perp Y_{S}\mid z,x^{\star},X_{S}, the support labels enter only through p⁡(z∣x⋆,XS,YS)p(z\!\mid\!x^{\star},X_{S},Y_{S}); the corruption probe in §3.1.1 measures the sensitivity of this posterior to perturbations in YSY_{S}. When the support adds little information beyond the unlabelled context, IΠ(z;YS∣x⋆,XS)≈0I_{\Pi}(z;Y_{S}\!\mid\!x^{\star},X_{S})\!\approx\!0, the posterior predictive collapses to a function of the unlabelled context alone, and a lazy / fixed-kernel solution can be population-optimal.

How existing relational ICL instantiates the relational prior?

What separates a relational prior from a tabular one is whether zz encodes cross-row dependence beyond i.i.d. rows. PluRel [32] and RDB-PFN [48] model this cross-row structure through a fixed bipartite hierarchical SBM [21, 29] for foreign keys plus a fixed family of cross-row aggregators (sum, max, min, mean, product, logsumexp) along a per-column DAG (Appendix E). These choices give PluRel a strong prior over schemas, FK topology, and per-column feature distributions. What is missing is an explicit relational dependence axis such as homophily sampled per episode as a varying latent that couples a row’s label to its FK-neighbours’ labels: the realised cross-row label dependence is hard-coded into the SCM rather than carried by such a latent, so under the standard ICL assumption the population-optimal predictor reduces to the support-independent marginal, i.e. the lazy regime.

Explicit relation-level modeling reproduces the feature-learning regime.

We inject a recurring relational latent into the label-generation process by replacing PluRel’s label step with a homophily-controlled mechanism: per database we sample a homophily target hh uniformly from a K=20K{=}20 grid spanning heterophily (h<0h{<}0) and homophily (h>0h{>}0) (using the adjusted relational homophily of Chen et al. [7]), and synthesise the label as a calibrated mixture of a cluster-driven and a feature-driven channel so that the realised homophily on the FK adjacency is monotone in hh, saturating in approximately [−0.44,+0.74][-0.44,\,+0.74] (Appendix G.1). Comparing these two processes, PluRel’s label-generating process can be written as

Y∼pPluRel​(Y∣E0,ξ),ξ∼p⁡(ξ),Y\;\sim\;p_{\mathrm{PluRel}}(Y\mid E_{0},\,\xi),\qquad\xi\sim p(\xi), (3)

where ξ=(schema,column SCM,FK-bipartite-HSBM,aggregator,…)\xi=(\text{schema},\text{column SCM},\text{FK-bipartite-HSBM},\text{aggregator},\dots). While ξ\xi does contain relational components, none of them is an explicit, recurring axis that directly controls the dependence between FK-adjacent labels: the realised cross-row label dependence is a downstream by-product of the SCM, not a latent shared across episodes that the support could identify. In our corruption probe (Table 2), PluRel-trained RT behaves as if the support-label correspondence carries little information about any recurring relational mechanism: shuffling labels and randomising features both yield near-inconsequential drops. We augment PluRel’s prior by factoring an explicit, finite, recurring relational latent hh alongside ξ\xi:

h∼Uniform⁡({h1,…,hK}),Y∼pours​(Y∣E0,ξ,h),h\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(\{h_{1},\dots,h_{K}\}),\qquad Y\;\sim\;p_{\mathrm{ours}}(Y\mid E_{0},\,\xi,\,h), (4)

so that p⁡(Y∣E0,h)p(Y\!\mid\!E_{0},h) realises a target relational dependence. The factor hh is concentrated, support-identifiable (I⁡(h;YS∣E0)>0I(h;Y_{S}\!\mid\!E_{0})\!>\!0 since FK-adjacent label co-occurrences reveal it), and relational (cannot be read from a single row), so the posterior p⁡(h∣E0,YS)p(h\!\mid\!E_{0},Y_{S}) moves with YSY_{S} and the predictor genuinely uses the support. This is the relational specialisation of latent-task accounts of ICL [54, 51, 58] and aligns with empirical evidence that ICL behaviour is shaped by the pre-training distribution itself [3, 20, 41]; the full theoretical treatment is in Appendix D.

Continual pre-training of RT-Plurel on this augmented corpus restores the feature-learning regime under purely synthetic supervision (RT-synth-diverse, Table 2). This recipe preserves PluRel’s schema and feature prior and only injects the missing relational-latent axis on top. Real held-out databases (RT-real-holdout) also escape the lazy regime via their own recurring latents, but those latents are unevenly sampled and they underperform despite operating in the right regime.

4 Improving existing RFM with these insights

Building on the diagnosis in Section 3, we introduce two modifications to RT: batch-level ICL addresses the context bottleneck identified in Section 3.1, and a diverse pre-training mixture addresses the lazy-regime bottleneck of Section 3.1.1.

4.1 Dual-stage In-Context Learning

Section 3.1 establishes that RT’s single-walk context is structurally impoverished on low-reachability tasks, and simply increasing the sampling sequence length LL brings almost no gain when the underlying subgraph is sparse in labeled task-table rows. As an alternative, we add a second in-context dimension: a batch-level attention operating across a batch of BB independently sampled queries (each carrying its own relational context). The in-context supervisory signal can now come from non-neighboring examples that are available regardless of walk structure. We refer to this architecture as dual-stage relational in-context learning. The remaining question is how to implement it efficiently. We identify two candidates: (1) end-to-end 2D attention, which jointly attends over the per-query relational context and the cross-query batch context in a single transformer with a full two-dimensional attention pattern—the most expressive option; (2) interleaving with existing tabular foundation model blocks, which alternates relational-context attention (within each query) and batch-context attention (across queries) layer by layer, preserving cross-query information flow at intermediate cost. For this design, we can view tabular foundation model as universal predictor over numerical values and reuse them. Option (1) is the most expressive yet fails in practice. Trained for 20,000 steps, its loss reaches 0.0100.010 while downstream regression collapses to R2=−4.3R^{2}\!=\!-4.3 with near-constant predictions. We attribute this to a bootstrapping problem: the backbone only gets a useful gradient once the batch-level head responds to in-context labels, and the head only gets one once the backbone produces query-discriminative embeddings.

Integration with TabICL. We instantiate the recipe with TabICL [39] and ablate the TabPFN [22] variant in Appendix C. TabICL is composed of three modules: a column encoder (ColEmbedding, a weight-shared encoder applied to each feature column), a row-interaction stage (RowInteraction, a permutation-invariant attention over cells within a row), and an ICL stage (ICLearning, a batch-level attention that conditions on the support labels). Most other tabular foundation models share this three-stage decomposition, so the integration recipe below transfers to them. The simplest architecture is the detached variant: we extract the pooled RT representation of each query and feed it into the full TabICL stack as if it were a row of an external table; alternatively we can bypass the column-encoder and row-interaction stages and apply only the ICLearning layer through a linear adapter. For higher expressiveness, we interleave ICLearning layers between RT blocks (Figure 2); this requires a dimension-matching adapter on each side of the spliced layer, which we activate by pre-training on held-out real-world databases. We conduct studies on these choices in Section 5.3.

Improving context length. TabICLv2’s context limit is only 20482048 rows, which is small compared to most large task tables that can scale to millions of rows. In practice, however, we find that this context size is already sufficient for most tasks (Section 5). When the effective context length does become a bottleneck, a simple and useful technique is support-level ensembling: rather than feeding a single support draw, we select multiple disjoint groups of support examples from the task table, run the model independently on each, and average the resulting predictions. This expands the effective number of support rows the prediction sees without changing the architecture. We ablate the trade-off between single-draw context size and ensembling in Section 5.3.

4.2 Better Pre-training Design

We continue pre-training from the PluRel checkpoint on a mixture of two corpora. (i) Real-world held-out databases. We use rel-amazon, dbinfer-outbrain-small, dbinfer-diginetica, and dbinfer-retailrocket, all disjoint from the evaluation tasks. Real-world databases provide useful signals for processing dense text embeddings. (ii) Homophily-aware synthetic corpus, as is described in Section 3.2. Real and synthetic are mixed at the episode level during pre-training.

Enhancing multi-class representations with a prototype objective.

RT’s cell-level readout heads cover only the binary and regression cases. To support the pre-training on multi-class tasks, we reuse RT’s existing readout via a prototype-based auxiliary objective [43]: within each batch we sample an NN-way episode, form per-class prototypes μc=|𝒮c|−1​∑i∈𝒮czi\mu_{c}=|\mathcal{S}_{c}|^{-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}_{c}}z_{i} from target-cell embeddings ziz_{i}, and train each query (xq,yq)(x_{q},y_{q}) with ℒproto=−log⁡softmaxc​(cos⁡(zq,μc)/τ)yq\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{proto}}=-\log\mathrm{softmax}_{c}\!\big(\cos(z_{q},\mu_{c})/\tau\big)_{y_{q}} at temperature τ\tau. On the rel-salt 16-way tasks (i-incot, s-shipc), this auxiliary lifts linear-probe accuracy by +0.04+0.04 over the binary/regression-only baseline.

5 Experiments

We evaluate our proposed model, OpenRFM, against strong baselines on a broad suite of predictive tasks drawn from RelBench-v1 [42], Kaggle, and RelBench-v2 [18]. We use the publicly reported numbers in these benchmarks to filter out tasks on which nearly all competent baselines already saturate or have potential leakage issues. The evaluation suite contains 2424 tasks in total: 1414 binary-classification tasks, 22 multi-class classification tasks, and 88 regression tasks. Each task is evaluated under both the autocomplete and regression settings introduced in §4.

Settings.

We compare OpenRFM against the following families of baselines: (1) training from scratch: per-task GNN-style models trained on each downstream task in isolation: RDL-GNN [42], NBFNet [59], RelGT [12], RT [40], and RelGNN [4]; (2) non-parametric RFM: JUICE [55] and RDB-PFN [48], a prior-data-fitted network pretrained on synthetic relational databases. We apply 88 group ensembling to these methods. (3) pre-trained relational transformer: RT-Plurel [32], pretrained on the PluRel synthetic corpus; and (4) “foundation model” that needs fine-tuning: Griffin [47], which only pre-trains the encoder on a set of real-world tabular data. It needs to be fine-tuned and does not support in-context learning. (5) the commercial RFM KumoRFMv1. Pre-training of OpenRFM is carried out on B200 GPUs and downstream task evaluation is conducted on a mixture of H100 and A6000 GPUs. To pretrain the RT backbone of OpenRFM, we find the best strategy is to continual pre-training from a PluRel checkpoint, which has already been pre-trained on 512512 synthetic databases with 1616b token costs. Training is using AdamW optimizer with a OneCycleLR schedule with batch size 128128, sequence length 10241024, and bf16 activations, run for 40 00040\,000 optimiser steps.

5.1 Overall ranking Results

Figure 3 gives the comparison across all 16 classification and 8 regression tasks. Missing cells (NS/OOM) are assigned the worst rank on that task. Full numerical results can be found in Appendix C. We observe: (1) OpenRFM is competitive across the board. Among all evaluated methods, OpenRFM attains a strong aggregate ranking on both classification and regression. (2) Relational ICL matches train-from-scratch with far smaller context. On t-fraud (rel-ieeecis), the training table has hundreds of thousands of rows, yet ICL methods (OpenRFM, KumoRFMv1) match train-from-scratch baselines using a limited support set. This suggests that for many predictive tasks the bottleneck is which mechanisms the support exposes, not how many rows are seen. (3) Parametric RFMs win when downstream signal is scarce. On smaller-scale databases such as rel-f1, where each task table provides limited labeled rows, parametric pre-trained models (OpenRFM, KumoRFMv1) clearly outperform both non-parametric ICL (JUICE) and train-from-scratch baselines. (4) Very-large-KK classification remains an open limitation. Tasks from rel-salt exceed the fixed class budget of TabICL-style readouts (10-way pre-trained head); we currently fall back to one versus all prediction. Closing this gap likely requires both architectural support for many-class readouts and pre-training data that exposes such priors at scale, a direction for follow-up work.

5.2 Pipeline efficiency

Beyond predictive accuracy, pipeline efficiency is also a critical consideration. We compare three paradigms — per-task train-from-scratch GNNs, the non-parametric JUICE pipeline, and OpenRFM — and decompose the wall-clock into (a) preparation (materialization, on-disk storage, and any task-specific training) and (b) inference latency. For the benchmark we pick rel-stack, a large-scale RelBench-v1 database with three task tables (u-badge, u-engage, p-votes), which exercises both per-task and per-database costs at realistic scale. All measurements are on a single NVIDIA RTX A6000 (48 GB) with an AMD EPYC 7763 64-core CPU and 1 TB of system memory.

As shown in Table 4, we observe: (1) the foundation-model paradigm is promising and clearly reduces task-specific preparation time compared to train-from-scratch baselines; (2) against the non-parametric Juice, parametric pre-training does not require per-task materialization and is therefore more storage-efficient; it is also more GPU-friendly and can natively handle dense embeddings produced by text or image foundation models; (3) on a single GPU, OpenRFM’s per-task inference is slower than a row-level GNN’s forward pass because cell-level cross-table attention is intrinsically more expensive, which is the price of performing relational ICL inside the model.

5.3 Ablation Studies

To better understand the components of OpenRFM, we further conduct ablation studies on three design dimensions: (1) pretraining, (2) relational ICL design, and (3) context selection.

(1) Pre-training corpus and objective.

We isolate the contribution of each ingredient. Holding the downstream pipeline (RT+TabICL, support size K=1024K{=}1024) fixed, we sweep six setups in Table 5: (a) the original RT-Plurel backbone; (b) adding TabICL batch-level attention on top of (a); (c) RT pre-trained with our prior plus TabICL; (d) (c) further augmented with real-world data; (e) (d) with the prototype auxiliary loss added; and (f) (e) with 8-seed support-side ensembling at inference. We report aggregate results by task family. The dual-stage in-context learning step contributes the largest single performance gain. Support-side ensembling, in contrast, yields only a marginal improvement on classification but a substantial one on regression. Moreover, blindly including real-world data hurts the performance, while organizing them with auxiliary prototype loss helps.

(2) Relational ICL design.

We next ask how the tabular ICL module should interact with RT. Table 6 compares four bridge designs: the detached bridge that feeds normalized final RT embeddings through the original TabICL encoder, the same bridge without normalization, a learned linear adapter that bypasses TabICL’s encoder and uses only ICLearning, and the best adapter-based interleaving over first, middle, and first-and-last RT positions. The evidence points to a simple design rule. Interleaving has limited and task-dependent benefit. By contrast, normalization is critical for stability: removing it makes some tasks drop a lot. The original TabICL encoder is much stronger than a linear RT→\rightarrowICLearning adapter. This results in our final design: RT connected to TabICL/TabPFN with a normalization layer in the middle.

(3) Context selection: support size, ensembling, and retrieval.

We then further explore the context selection strategy. Backbone setting is identical to 5.3’s (1). We consider support size K∈{256,512,1024}K\!\in\!\{256,512,1024\}, ensemble breadth E∈{1,8}E\!\in\!\{1,8\}, and the selection rule (random, balanced, temporal). temporal picks the KK most recent train rows by parquet timestamp. We report on two representative tasks: rel-stack/u-badge (∼\sim5% positive class) and rel-ieeecis/t-fraud (clf, AUC; ∼\sim3.4% positive). Two trends emerge: (i) ensembling (E=8E{=}8) consistently adds AUC. On the imbalanced u-badge it stabilizes balanced-controller variance; (ii) the balanced controller dominates at large KK, achieving the best AUC on both tasks, which is eventually our support selection strategy. Here, we only consider query-agnostic context selection considering the KVcache. Query-aware context selection is a meaningful future work.

6 Conclusion and Discussion

We diagnose two bottlenecks in open RFMs — relation-level label scarcity and a lazy pre-training regime — and address them with dual-stage ICL and a homophily-aware synthetic-plus-real mixture. Together they define OpenRFM, a single open backbone that improves average performance by ∼30%{\sim}30\% over RT and surpasses the commercial KumoRFMv1 on most evaluation tasks.

Discussion: deeper understanding of relation-level and batch-level treatment.

One phenomenon we observe but do not yet fully understand is that the gap between RT-Plurel and RT-diverse-syn shrinks once a batch-level attention head is attached on top: even a relatively weak relational backbone becomes competitive when it is paired with a pre-trained tabular ICL layer. We believe reusing an existing tabular foundation model is the right direction, but the mechanism behind this complementarity — in particular which signal each stage actually contributes, and whether there is a tighter coupling that does better than the current splice — remains open, and we leave a more principled study of the combination to future work.

Discussion: extending to recommendation.

The pipeline does not extend automatically to recommendation. KumoRFM v1 handles it via an NBFNet-like row-level graph transformer with an inductive feature encoder [16], but such models underperform on general recommendation (e.g., Amazon-book [57]) where transductive id-based methods dominate; KumoRFM v2 omits recommendation entirely [23]. It’s challenging to design recommendation foundation model since the discriminative signal for recommendation lives in the relational structure, not in raw cells. We sketch an agent-RFM pipeline in which a coding agent materialises relational signals into per-pair tabular features, after which the standard pipeline applies; Appendix I demonstrates this on rel-hm/user-item-purchase, reaching MAP@1212 comparable to KumoRFM v1 and to transductive NBFNet baselines.

Appendix A Broader Impacts

OpenRFM is a foundational predictive model over relational databases. On the positive side, by open-sourcing the model and its synthetic-data pipeline, we lower the engineering barrier to relational predictive modelling and provide a strong non-commercial baseline accessible to researchers and organisations without bespoke ML teams. On the risk side, OpenRFM inherits the standard concerns of any tabular/relational predictor deployed on consequential decisions—fairness, privacy of in-context support records, and over-reliance on in-context predictions in high-stakes settings—and downstream users should audit accordingly.

Appendix B More Related Works

Relational deep learning.

The RDL paradigm builds on graph neural networks (GNNs) as the primary modeling tool, with RelBench [42, 18] and 4DBInfer [46] providing a standardized benchmark. Recent advances include composite message passing schemes that capture higher-order relational patterns [4] and specialized architectures for recommendation over relational databases [57]. Transformers and large language models have also been explored for relational prediction [12, 52, 53], though they tend to be resource-heavy with modest performance gains. Related efforts such as AutoG [6] and RDB2G-Bench [9] address an upstream bottleneck for the entire RDL stack: they study how a database should be turned into a graph in the first place, either by automatically generating schemas with LLM-driven transformations (AutoG) or by benchmarking the choice of graph modelling against downstream task quality (RDB2G-Bench).

Prior-fitted networks for graphs.

A separate line of recent work transplants the PFN recipe to graph node classification. This shares some similarity to relational ICL since both of them can be seen as a 2D ICL problem. G2T-FM [13] adapts a tabular foundation model such as TabPFN to graphs by aggregating neighbour features into the row of a synthetic table and reusing the tabular ICL engine. GraphPFN [14] pre-trains a tabular backbone augmented with attention-based neighbourhood aggregation on synthetic graphs drawn from a hierarchical SBM plus preferential-attachment prior. NodePFN [10] pre-trains a context-query attention architecture with local message passing on thousands of synthetic graphs. These three share the high-level PFN philosophy with our work but operate in a different in-context regime: the support set is constructed at the node level (the model sees an entire small graph plus a labelled subset of its nodes), and the labels enter as a separate input channel rather than as cells inside the unrolled sequence. The relational walks we consider, by contrast, treat support labels as cells inside the BFS-unrolled context (Section 2.2). Empirically, the graph-PFN line has so far been evaluated on small-to-medium-scale benchmarks with at most ∼105\sim\!10^{5} nodes per graph.

Graph foundation models and the geometric-symmetry route.

A parallel line of work pursues graph foundation models through the lens of geometric symmetry. ULTRA [17] learns transferable knowledge-graph representations by conditioning on a relation graph and applying NBFNet-style message passing, reaching strong zero-shot transfer across different KGs. Mao et al. [33] and Wang et al. [49] considers building a single backbone whose architecture respects the relevant symmetries (permutation, relabeling, and structure-level invariances) so that one pre-trained model transfers to any graph. The empirical record so far is that convincing zero-shot transfer has been observed almost exclusively on knowledge-graph reasoning tasks (entity-pair link prediction over a fixed relation vocabulary), while transfer to general node-, link-prediction has remained much harder. Bevilacqua et al. [2] go further and argue that this is structural rather than empirical: different task levels (node, edge, higher-order) require different permutation symmetries that are difficult to reconcile inside a single backbone, so a symmetry-respecting universal architecture is intrinsically constrained.

Appendix D Theoretical Discussion of Section 3

This appendix formalises the claims in Section 3 about when a relational transformer (RT) actually learns from in-context support labels. We organise the theory around three points that mirror the empirical observations. (i) RT pre-training is prior-data fitting [34, 35, 22]; in the lazy / NTK regime [25, 8] it reduces to a fixed-kernel predictor over relational episodes. (ii) The pre-training prior places RT in either the lazy or the feature-learning regime through a single statistical property: whether support labels are posterior-informative about a recurring relational latent. (iii) Homophily is one instantiation of such a latent; the marginal spread of any scalar homophily statistic is neither necessary nor sufficient for feature-learning ICL. Throughout, 𝔼Π\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}, HΠH_{\Pi}, IΠI_{\Pi} denote expectation, entropy, mutual information under prior Π\Pi. Random variables are upper-case, realisations lower-case.

D.1 Relational prior-data fitting and the lazy kernel limit

Setup.

A relational episode is a tuple E=(E0,YS,Yq)E=(E_{0},Y_{S},Y_{q}) where qq is the query row, S={1,…,m}S=\{1,\dots,m\} indexes the labelled support rows reachable from qq through the relational context, YS=(Y1,…,Ym)Y_{S}=(Y_{1},\dots,Y_{m}) are their labels, and YqY_{q} is the query label. The unlabelled context E0=(q,G,X,A,S)E_{0}=(q,G,X,A,S) collects the sampled relational neighbourhood GG, non-label cells XX, structural addresses A=(A1,…,Am)A=(A_{1},\dots,A_{m}) (table identity, hop distance, FK path, timestamp bucket, label-column role), and the support index set SS. A relational pre-training prior Π\Pi is a distribution over data-generating mechanisms η=(ξ,z)\eta=(\xi,z), where ξ\xi encodes nuisance structure (schema, column distributions, noise) and zz is the episode-level relational mechanism — a path-conditioned aggregation rule, a temporal window, a label-compatibility matrix, or a homophily level. Conditional on η\eta, episodes are drawn from PηP_{\eta}. Pre-training minimises

ℛΠ​(f)=𝔼η∼Π​𝔼E∼Pη​[ℓ⁡(f⁡(E0,YS),Yq)].\mathcal{R}_{\Pi}(f)=\mathbb{E}_{\eta\sim\Pi}\,\mathbb{E}_{E\sim P_{\eta}}\!\big[\ell\big(f(E_{0},Y_{S}),\,Y_{q}\big)\big]. (5)

Under log loss, the population minimiser is the posterior predictive

qΠ⋆​(y∣E0,YS)=∫pη​(Yq=y∣E0,YS)​Π​(𝑑η∣E0,YS),q_{\Pi}^{\star}(y\mid E_{0},Y_{S})=\int p_{\eta}(Y_{q}{=}y\mid E_{0},Y_{S})\,\Pi(\mathrm{d}\eta\mid E_{0},Y_{S}), (6)

and under squared loss it is 𝔼Π[Yq∣E0,YS]\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}[Y_{q}\mid E_{0},Y_{S}]. To see this, marginalise η\eta via the tower property to obtain

pΠ​(Yq∣E0,YS)=∫pη​(Yq∣E0,YS)​Π​(𝑑η∣E0,YS),p_{\Pi}(Y_{q}\mid E_{0},Y_{S})=\int p_{\eta}(Y_{q}\mid E_{0},Y_{S})\,\Pi(\mathrm{d}\eta\mid E_{0},Y_{S}), (7)

and rewrite (5) as

ℛΠ(f)=𝔼(E0,YS)[𝔼Yq∼pΠ(⋅∣E0,YS)[ℓ(f(E0,YS),Yq)]].\mathcal{R}_{\Pi}(f)=\mathbb{E}_{(E_{0},Y_{S})}\!\Big[\,\mathbb{E}_{Y_{q}\sim p_{\Pi}(\cdot\mid E_{0},Y_{S})}\!\big[\ell(f(E_{0},Y_{S}),\,Y_{q})\big]\Big]. (8)

For log loss the inner expectation is the cross-entropy H(pΠ,f)=H(pΠ)+KL(pΠ∥f)\mathrm{H}(p_{\Pi},f)=\mathrm{H}(p_{\Pi})+\mathrm{KL}(p_{\Pi}\,\|\,f), minimised pointwise at f=pΠf=p_{\Pi} by Gibbs’ inequality. For squared loss the same decomposition gives 𝔼[(Yq−f)2∣E0,YS]=Var[Yq∣E0,YS]+(f−𝔼[Yq∣E0,YS])2\mathbb{E}[(Y_{q}-f)^{2}\mid E_{0},Y_{S}]=\mathrm{Var}[Y_{q}\mid E_{0},Y_{S}]+(f-\mathbb{E}[Y_{q}\mid E_{0},Y_{S}])^{2}, minimised at f=𝔼Π[Yq∣E0,YS]f=\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}[Y_{q}\mid E_{0},Y_{S}]. A trained RT is therefore an amortised Bayes act for the statistical experiment induced by Π\Pi [34, 35, 22, 54].

The label-transfer kernel.

The corruption probes of Section 3.1.1 ask how the RT prediction changes when the support is perturbed. To first order, label perturbations are captured by the label-transfer kernel

Γθ,i​(E)=∂fθ​(E0,YS)∂Yi,Γθ​(E)∈ℝm,\Gamma_{\theta,i}(E)=\frac{\partial f_{\theta}(E_{0},Y_{S})}{\partial Y_{i}},\qquad\Gamma_{\theta}(E)\in\mathbb{R}^{m}, (9)

where fθ​(E)f_{\theta}(E) is the scalar pre-logit of the RT. The derivative is taken with respect to the continuous label-cell embeddings used by the RT tokenizer, so Γθ\Gamma_{\theta} is well-defined for both regression labels and embedded categorical labels. Both the label-shuffle and the feature-shuffle probes are linear functionals of Γθ\Gamma_{\theta}, so claims about the empirical regime translate directly into claims about Γθ\Gamma_{\theta}.

For each address aa, let Ca={i:Ai=a}C_{a}=\{i:A_{i}=a\}, and define the address-pooling projection and its complement

Theorem 1 is a first-order, within-address idealisation of the empirical corruption protocol of Section 3.1.1: it relates the linearised sensitivities DshuffleD_{\mathrm{shuffle}} and DfeatD_{\mathrm{feat}} to the squared norms of the row-specific component Γθrel\Gamma_{\theta}^{\mathrm{rel}} under the stated invariance and moment assumptions. We use it interpretively from this point on: the assertion “RT is in the lazy / frozen-feature regime” is identified with the assertion ‖Γθrel​(E0)‖2≈0\|\Gamma_{\theta}^{\mathrm{rel}}(E_{0})\|_{2}\approx 0. The remaining question is when this holds at the population minimiser of (5), which is the subject of the next subsection.

D.2 Posterior identifiability and the feature-learning transition

We now characterise when a prior makes support labels statistically useful — when the population-optimal predictor genuinely depends on YSY_{S} through row-specific channels rather than through address-pooled statistics alone.

Definition 2 (Support-identifiable relational latent).

A latent zz is a support-identifiable relational latent under Π\Pi if it satisfies:

  • •

    Recurrence: z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z} for an effectively finite family reused across episodes [54, in the sense of finite-capacity ICL contexts;];

  • •

    Support identifiability: IΠ​(z;YS∣E0)>0I_{\Pi}(z;Y_{S}\mid E_{0})>0;

  • •

    Relationality: zz is not measurable with respect to query-local features alone, i.e. z∉σ⁡(q,Xq)z\notin\sigma(q,X_{q}).

Recurrence distinguishes a prior from a single noise draw: without it, zz is a fresh nuisance per episode and cannot be amortised. Support identifiability is the data-processing property that makes YSY_{S} informative. Relationality rules out latents an architecture without relational context could already recover from a single row. Definition 2 specialises latent-task accounts of in-context learning [54, 51, 58] to the relational setting: demonstrations are useful when they identify a recurring task/mechanism latent, but here that latent must be recoverable specifically through relational support labels.

Assumption 3 (Latent Markov structure).

Conditional on E0E_{0} and zz, the support and query labels decouple:

Yq⟂⟂YS|E0,z.Y_{q}\;\perp\!\!\!\perp\;Y_{S}\;\Big|\;E_{0},\,z. (13)

This is the structural assumption underlying topic-model and Bayesian latent-variable accounts of in-context learning [54, 58]: YSY_{S} and YqY_{q} are conditionally independent given the episode mechanism.

Theorem 4 (Inert support implies a permutation-invariant Bayes act).

Under Assumption 3, if IΠ​(z;YS∣E0)=0I_{\Pi}(z;Y_{S}\mid E_{0})=0, then

pΠ​(Yq∣E0,YS)=pΠ​(Yq∣E0),p_{\Pi}(Y_{q}\mid E_{0},Y_{S})=p_{\Pi}(Y_{q}\mid E_{0}), (14)

and consequently 𝔼Π[Yq∣E0,YS]=𝔼Π[Yq∣E0]\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}[Y_{q}\mid E_{0},Y_{S}]=\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}[Y_{q}\mid E_{0}] and ∂YS𝔼Π[Yq∣E0,YS]=0\partial_{Y_{S}}\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}[Y_{q}\mid E_{0},Y_{S}]=0.

Proof.

Mutual information vanishes iff the conditional distribution is unchanged, so Π⁡(d​z∣E0,YS)=Π⁡(d​z∣E0)\Pi(\mathrm{d}z\mid E_{0},Y_{S})=\Pi(\mathrm{d}z\mid E_{0}). Marginalising under (13),

pΠ​(Yq∣E0,YS)=∫p⁡(Yq∣E0,z)​Π​(𝑑z∣E0,YS)=∫p⁡(Yq∣E0,z)​Π​(𝑑z∣E0)=pΠ​(Yq∣E0).p_{\Pi}(Y_{q}\mid E_{0},Y_{S})=\int p(Y_{q}\mid E_{0},z)\,\Pi(\mathrm{d}z\mid E_{0},Y_{S})=\int p(Y_{q}\mid E_{0},z)\,\Pi(\mathrm{d}z\mid E_{0})=p_{\Pi}(Y_{q}\mid E_{0}).

Differentiating in YSY_{S} gives the second claim. ∎

Theorem 4 makes the lazy regime causal rather than incidental: when the prior is posterior-inert, the Bayes-optimal predictor ignores row–label correspondence. A lazy fixed-kernel solution is then statistically sufficient, not a pathology of optimisation.

Remark.

Reading Theorem 4 through the kernel formalism of Subsection D.1: under the conditions of the theorem, the population minimiser of (5) satisfies Γrel,⋆​(E0)=0\Gamma^{\mathrm{rel},\star}(E_{0})=0 for almost every E0E_{0}, since ∂YS𝔼Π[Yq∣E0,YS]=0\partial_{Y_{S}}\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}[Y_{q}\mid E_{0},Y_{S}]=0. By Theorem 1, both DshuffleD_{\mathrm{shuffle}} and DfeatD_{\mathrm{feat}} vanish at the optimum. The lazy / frozen-feature signature observed empirically under synthetic-only pre-training (Table 2) is therefore the corruption-probe footprint of the population Bayes act on a support-inert prior, not an architectural artefact of training.

Address-pooled versus row-specific transfer.

We work with a local model of the label-transfer kernel that splits address-aggregate transfer from a learnable row-specific direction:

Γu,i​(E)=γ⁡(Ai,B⁡(E0))⏟address-pooled channel+u⊤​ϕi​(E0)⏟row-specific channel,\Gamma_{u,i}(E)\;=\;\underbrace{\gamma\!\big(A_{i},\,B(E_{0})\big)}_{\text{address-pooled channel}}\;+\;\underbrace{u^{\top}\phi_{i}(E_{0})}_{\text{row-specific channel}}, (15)

where γ\gamma depends only on the structural address AiA_{i} and an invariant context statistic B⁡(E0)B(E_{0}), ϕi​(E0)∈ℝd\phi_{i}(E_{0})\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is a centred relational feature for the query–support pair (q,i)(q,i), and u∈ℝdu\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is the row-specific parameter. The centring condition

∑i:Ai=aϕi(E0)= 0∀a,\sum_{i\,:\,A_{i}=a}\phi_{i}(E_{0})\;=\;0\quad\forall\,a, (16)

enforced by per-address standardisation in the RT readout, makes ϕi\phi_{i} orthogonal to the address-pooling projection Πagg\Pi_{\mathrm{agg}}. Define the address-pooled residual and the row-feature signal

rγ​(E)=Yq−b⁡(E0)−∑iγ⁡(Ai,B⁡(E0))​Yi,T⁡(E)=∑iYi​ϕi​(E0)∈ℝd,r_{\gamma}(E)\;=\;Y_{q}-b(E_{0})-\sum_{i}\gamma\!\big(A_{i},B(E_{0})\big)\,Y_{i},\qquad T(E)\;=\;\sum_{i}Y_{i}\,\phi_{i}(E_{0})\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{d}, (17)

and consider the population ridge risk in the row-specific direction

ℛ⁡(γ,u)=12​𝔼Π​[(rγ​(E)−u⊤​T​(E))2]+λ2​‖u‖22(λ>0).\mathcal{R}(\gamma,u)\;=\;\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}\!\Big[\big(r_{\gamma}(E)-u^{\top}T(E)\big)^{2}\Big]\;+\;\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\,\|u\|_{2}^{2}\qquad(\lambda>0). (18)
Assumption 5 (Realisable relational signal).

There exists κ>0\kappa>0 such that ‖𝔼Π​[rγ​(E)​T​(E)]‖2≥κ\big\|\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}[r_{\gamma}(E)\,T(E)]\big\|_{2}\geq\kappa.

Theorem 6 (Nonzero residual–support covariance forces feature learning).

Under Assumption 5, the address-pooled subspace {u=0}\{u=0\} is not stationary for ℛ\mathcal{R}:

∇uℛ​(γ,0)=−𝔼Π​[rγ​(E)​T​(E)]≠0.\nabla_{u}\mathcal{R}(\gamma,0)=-\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}[r_{\gamma}(E)\,T(E)]\neq 0. (19)

Moreover, gradient flow u˙t=−∇uℛ​(γ,ut)\dot{u}_{t}=-\nabla_{u}\mathcal{R}(\gamma,u_{t}) initialised at u0=0u_{0}=0 satisfies

‖ut‖2≥κ2​t∀t∈(0,t0),\|u_{t}\|_{2}\geq\tfrac{\kappa}{2}\,t\quad\forall\,t\in(0,t_{0}), (20)

for some t0>0t_{0}>0 depending on the smoothness of ℛ\mathcal{R}.

Proof.

Differentiating (18) in uu,

∇uℛ​(γ,u)=−𝔼Π​[(rγ​(E)−u⊤​T​(E))​T​(E)]+λ​u,\nabla_{u}\mathcal{R}(\gamma,u)\;=\;-\,\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}\!\big[(r_{\gamma}(E)-u^{\top}T(E))\,T(E)\big]+\lambda\,u,

so ∇uℛ​(γ,0)=−𝔼Π​[rγ​(E)​T​(E)]\nabla_{u}\mathcal{R}(\gamma,0)=-\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}[r_{\gamma}(E)\,T(E)], which is nonzero by Assumption 5. The gradient flow ut=u0−t​∇uℛ​(γ,0)+O⁡(t2)u_{t}=u_{0}-t\,\nabla_{u}\mathcal{R}(\gamma,0)+O(t^{2}) with u0=0u_{0}=0 and ‖∇uℛ​(γ,0)‖2≥κ\|\nabla_{u}\mathcal{R}(\gamma,0)\|_{2}\geq\kappa gives (20). ∎

Theorem 6 is the dynamical counterpart of Theorem 4: when residual–support covariance is bounded away from zero, gradient-based pre-training is repelled from the lazy / address-pooled subspace. This is the same mechanism by which feature learning escapes lazy / NTK behaviour in the supervised setting [25, 8, 56], specialised to the relational ICL geometry of (15).

Remark.

Theorem 6 is a statement about the population gradient at u=0u=0, not a convergence result. The conclusion that the row-specific direction is excited carries over to a finite-step optimiser provided the empirical covariance approximates 𝔼Π​[rγ​T]\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}[r_{\gamma}T] to within κ/2\kappa/2, which holds under standard concentration on Π\Pi. We do not claim a finite-sample rate or that the trained RT reaches the population minimiser; we only claim that its trajectory cannot remain on the address-pooled subspace.

Information-theoretic restatement.

Define the in-context information ΔICL:=IΠ​(Yq;YS∣E0)\Delta_{\mathrm{ICL}}:=I_{\Pi}(Y_{q};Y_{S}\mid E_{0}). Under Assumption 3, the data-processing inequality on the chain YS→z→YqY_{S}\to z\to Y_{q} (conditional on E0E_{0}) gives

ΔICL≤min⁡{IΠ​(z;YS∣E0),IΠ​(z;Yq∣E0)}.\Delta_{\mathrm{ICL}}\;\leq\;\min\!\big\{\,I_{\Pi}(z;Y_{S}\mid E_{0}),\;\;I_{\Pi}(z;Y_{q}\mid E_{0})\,\big\}. (21)

Both factors must be nonzero for support labels to add Bayes value: a recurring relational latent that is identifiable from YSY_{S} and predictive of YqY_{q}. This is the population-level signature of the lazy-to-feature-learning transition observed in Section 3.2.

D.3 Homophily, recurrence, and the inadequacy of marginal diversity

The previous section identifies the causal property — a recurring, support-identifiable, relational latent — without reference to homophily. We now show that homophily is one clean instantiation of that property, but that the marginal spread of homophily statistics is not the property itself.

Homophily as a relational latent.

Let z=h∈{h1,…,hK}z=h\in\{h_{1},\dots,h_{K}\} be a finite homophily target controlling label compatibility along FK neighbourhoods, in the spirit of the planted-partition / SBM family [21, 29, 7]. Conditional on hh, FK-adjacent rows have label agreement / disagreement rates determined by hh. Our use of homophily as a recurring episode-level latent is related to adjusted homophily and label informativeness as graph-dataset descriptors [38], and to the older statistical-relational-learning notion of relational autocorrelation [26, 36], where labels of linked entities are statistically dependent through latent relational structure. The difference is that in our setting hh is a controlled, support-identifiable latent during pre-training rather than a post-hoc dataset statistic.

Corollary 7 (Homophily induces feature-learning ICL when used as a latent).

If hh is pinned per episode, recurs across episodes, is identifiable from YSY_{S}, and is predictive of YqY_{q}, then I⁡(h;YS∣E0)>0I(h;Y_{S}\mid E_{0})>0 and I⁡(h;Yq∣E0)>0I(h;Y_{q}\mid E_{0})>0. Under Assumption 5, the address-pooled subspace is unstable and pre-training enters feature learning by Theorem 6.

Proof.

Finite support of hh supplies recurrence. FK-neighbourhood label agreement makes YSY_{S} informative about hh, hence I⁡(h;YS∣E0)>0I(h;Y_{S}\mid E_{0})>0. Since hh controls YqY_{q} through the same FK-neighbourhood compatibility mechanism, I⁡(h;Yq∣E0)>0I(h;Y_{q}\mid E_{0})>0. The conclusion follows from Theorem 6. ∎

The corollary does not say homophily is the unique mechanism that satisfies Definition 2: any recurring, support-identifiable relational latent suffices.

Remark.

Definition 2 is a cheap test: given a candidate latent it is straightforward to check whether the three conditions hold and Theorem 6 applies. Identifying which candidates actually qualify in a given relational generator, however, is empirical. As one cautionary example, the set of aggregation primitives that simulates DFS-style operators (sum/count/mean/max along an FK path) is a natural candidate for zz, but in practice it does not behave as a recurring relational latent under the corruption probe: the realised aggregator can be read off feature-only summaries of E0E_{0}, so the support-identifiability condition I⁡(z;YS∣E0)>0I(z;Y_{S}\!\mid\!E_{0})\!>\!0 fails. Definition 2 is therefore best read as a falsifiable structural criterion rather than a constructive recipe; finding informative relational latents for a particular generator is itself an empirical task.

Marginal spread is neither necessary nor sufficient.

Let H⁡(E)H(E) be a scalar episode statistic, e.g. a relational-homophily summary in the sense of Chen et al. [7], and define its marginal spread as SpreadH​(Π)=VarE∼Π​[H⁡(E)]\mathrm{Spread}_{H}(\Pi)=\mathrm{Var}_{E\sim\Pi}[H(E)]. The motivation for separating the marginal-spread of HH from the underlying causal property echoes the warning in Platonov et al. [38] that simple homophily measures can be misleading and that label informativeness is the more meaningful quantity.

Theorem 8 (Marginal HH-spread is decoupled from the support-identifiability surrogate).

There exist priors Π1,Π2,Π3\Pi_{1},\Pi_{2},\Pi_{3} on episodes EE and an associated mediating latents such that the data-processing inequality (21) applies on each, and

  • •

    (Insufficiency) SpreadH​(Π1)=SpreadH​(Π2)\mathrm{Spread}_{H}(\Pi_{1})=\mathrm{Spread}_{H}(\Pi_{2}), but IΠ1​(z;YS∣E0)=0I_{\Pi_{1}}(z;Y_{S}\mid E_{0})=0 while IΠ2​(z;YS∣E0)>0I_{\Pi_{2}}(z;Y_{S}\mid E_{0})>0;

  • •

    (Non-necessity) SpreadH​(Π3)=0\mathrm{Spread}_{H}(\Pi_{3})=0, but IΠ3​(z;YS∣E0)>0I_{\Pi_{3}}(z;Y_{S}\mid E_{0})>0.

Proof.

Insufficiency. Let Π1\Pi_{1} draw episodes with the latent z≡z0z\equiv z_{0} constant, so Π1\Pi_{1} generates YS,YqY_{S},Y_{q} from p(⋅∣E0,z0)p(\cdot\mid E_{0},z_{0}), and let H⁡(E)H(E) be a deterministic function of E0E_{0} alone with non-degenerate distribution under Π1\Pi_{1}. Then SpreadH​(Π1)>0\mathrm{Spread}_{H}(\Pi_{1})>0, but since zz is constant, IΠ1​(z;YS∣E0)=0I_{\Pi_{1}}(z;Y_{S}\mid E_{0})=0 trivially. Now let Π2\Pi_{2} satisfy Definition 2 with Markov structure as in Assumption 3 for a recurring relational latent z′z^{\prime}, and append a statistic H′​(E)≡H⁡(E0)H^{\prime}(E)\equiv H(E_{0}) that depends only on E0E_{0} and is therefore not a mediator, with SpreadH′​(Π2)=SpreadH​(Π1)\mathrm{Spread}_{H^{\prime}}(\Pi_{2})=\mathrm{Spread}_{H}(\Pi_{1}). By Definition 2, IΠ2​(z′;YS∣E0)>0I_{\Pi_{2}}(z^{\prime};Y_{S}\mid E_{0})>0, while the marginal spread of the chosen statistic matches Π1\Pi_{1} by construction.

Non-necessity. Let Π3\Pi_{3} satisfy Definition 2 for a recurring relational latent z′z^{\prime} (e.g. a finite path-aggregation rule or a temporal-window mechanism), and pick HH to be almost surely constant under Π3\Pi_{3} — for instance, H⁡(E)≡h0H(E)\equiv h_{0} for all EE in the support of Π3\Pi_{3}. Then SpreadH​(Π3)=0\mathrm{Spread}_{H}(\Pi_{3})=0 by construction, while IΠ3​(z′;YS∣E0)>0I_{\Pi_{3}}(z^{\prime};Y_{S}\mid E_{0})>0 by Definition 2. ∎

By Theorem 4, IΠ​(z;YS∣E0)=0I_{\Pi}(z;Y_{S}\mid E_{0})=0 implies IΠ​(Yq;YS∣E0)=0I_{\Pi}(Y_{q};Y_{S}\mid E_{0})=0, so the insufficiency direction transfers to the Bayes-relevant quantity IΠ​(Yq;YS∣E0)I_{\Pi}(Y_{q};Y_{S}\mid E_{0}). The converse, that IΠ​(z;YS∣E0)>0I_{\Pi}(z;Y_{S}\mid E_{0})>0 alone yields IΠ​(Yq;YS∣E0)>0I_{\Pi}(Y_{q};Y_{S}\mid E_{0})>0, additionally requires zz to be predictive of YqY_{q}, i.e. IΠ​(z;Yq∣E0)>0I_{\Pi}(z;Y_{q}\mid E_{0})>0; this is not implied by Definition 2 on its own but is verified separately for our constructions of Π2\Pi_{2} and Π3\Pi_{3} via Corollary 7. We state Theorem 8 on the surrogate IΠ​(z;YS∣E0)I_{\Pi}(z;Y_{S}\mid E_{0}) because it is the cleanest formal expression of the decoupling between marginal HH-spread and feature learning.

Theorem 8 is the formal statement behind the data-side narrative in Section 3.2: homophily helps when deployed as a recurring, support-identifiable relational latent. The marginal histogram of any homophily statistic is a downstream summary, not a cause. This formalises, in our relational setting, the broader observation that ICL behaviour is strongly shaped by distributional properties of the pre-training data [3].

Remark.

Theorem 8 explains the apparent paradox that the realised homophily of PluRel-generated databases already covers a non-trivial range, yet PluRel-only pre-training stays in the lazy regime. Although the marginal HH-spread is not small, PluRel does not introduce a homophily-controlling latent during the label-generation phase: the realised homophily of any episode is a downstream summary statistic of the SCM equations and the bipartite-HSBM matching, not a sampled, recurring quantity that controls YqY_{q} across episodes. PluRel is therefore a concrete instance of Π1\Pi_{1} in the insufficiency construction — HH varies, but the surrogate IΠ​(z;YS∣E0)I_{\Pi}(z;Y_{S}\mid E_{0}) is essentially zero — which is why the corruption probe in Table 2 reads as lazy regardless of how wide the homophily histogram is.

Appendix E PluRel Synthetic Pre-training Data

This section gives the full description of the PluRel [32] synthetic data generator referenced in Section 2.2. Each episode is a freshly sampled (database, task) pair; the procedural prior used by the public PluRel implementation is summarised in Table 9.

The same (G,X)(G,X) pipeline is reused unchanged in our diverse-synthetic corpus; only the task / label stage is replaced by an explicit homophily-controlled mechanism, as described in Appendix G.

Appendix F Dataset Details

F.1 Pre-training and Evaluation Split

Table 10 summarizes the assignment of relational databases to pre-training and evaluation sets. Pre-training databases are used to train the OpenRFM backbone and ICL head; evaluation databases are held out entirely and used only for zero-shot or few-shot evaluation. No evaluation database is seen during pre-training.

Appendix G Designing Diversity in the Relational Prior

This appendix describes the diversity intervention referenced in Section 3.2. The intervention modifies only the supervision channel of the procedural prior: the schema, foreign-key wiring, and per-column feature population produced by PluRel’s structural causal model are reused unchanged, and our corpus differs from PluRel only in how the target label yy is generated. Holding (G,X)(G,X) fixed isolates the homophily axis from confounds in feature distribution or schema topology.

G.1 Homophily diversity

Hierarchical block model with controlled homophily.

We parameterise the homophily axis by a target h∈[−1,+1]h\in[-1,+1]. For each target table t⋆t^{\star} we recover a two-level block hierarchy (b(1),b(2))(b^{(1)},b^{(2)}) from the FK topology, where br(1)b^{(1)}_{r} is the parent block of row rr and br(2)b^{(2)}_{r} is a sub-block within it. The label of row rr is a mixture of a cluster-driven and a feature-driven channel:

yr={yr(c),w.p. ​|h|,yr(f),w.p. ​1−|h|,yr(c)={br(1)mod2,h>0,(br(1)mod2)⊕(br(2)mod2),h<0,y_{r}=\begin{cases}y^{(c)}_{r},&\text{w.p. }|h|,\\ y^{(f)}_{r},&\text{w.p. }1-|h|,\end{cases}\qquad y^{(c)}_{r}=\begin{cases}b^{(1)}_{r}\bmod 2,&h>0,\\ (b^{(1)}_{r}\bmod 2)\oplus(b^{(2)}_{r}\bmod 2),&h<0,\end{cases} (22)

where yr(f)∼Bern⁡(σ⁡(β​ϕ​(xr)))y^{(f)}_{r}\sim\mathrm{Bern}(\sigma(\beta\,\phi(x_{r}))) is a feature-driven channel (ϕ\phi a random projection of rr’s numeric features) and ⊕\oplus denotes XOR. Eq. (22) is defined for h≠0h\neq 0; the corpus grid below excludes h=0h=0 so y(c)y^{(c)} is always well-defined. The construction has two intentional properties. (i) When h>0h>0, FK-adjacent rows that share a parent block share a label, producing homophilic structure of magnitude proportional to hh. (ii) When h<0h<0, the XOR with the sub-block parity flips the label between sibling sub-blocks, producing structurally heterophilic targets at the same FK adjacencies, rather than the noise-style heterophily a permutation produces. As |h|→0|h|\to 0 the cluster channel is mixed in with vanishing weight, so the label degenerates smoothly to the feature-only limit yr=yr(f)y_{r}=y^{(f)}_{r} on either side. The mixture in (22) thus sweeps between feature-only and structure-only labels along a single scalar.

Corpus construction.

We instantiate this construction as the diverse-synthetic corpus used throughout the paper. For each generated database we sample K=21K=21 homophily targets equispaced in [−1,+1][-1,+1] and emit one label column per target on the same (G,X)(G,X). Concretely, given an episode produced by the PluRel procedural prior, we build the block hierarchy and feature projection once, then run Algorithm 1 to overlay 2121 label columns indexed by their homophily tags. Each (G,X)(G,X) thus appears 2121 times in the corpus, paired with 2121 different homophily levels, which is what makes the homophily target a recurring, support-identifiable, relational latent in the sense of Definition 2.

Realised homophily and saturation.

We verify the construction by measuring the realised adjusted homophily h^​(𝐲)\hat{h}(\mathbf{y}) on the FK-adjacency edge set. The realised range therefore covers a wide but bounded interval of approximately [−0.44,+0.74][-0.44,+0.74], which we find sufficient to cross out of the lazy regime in Section 3.2.

Implementation.

The synthetic generator is reimplemented from scratch in Rust to make corpus-scale generation tractable. We re-write the schema sampler, the bipartite hierarchical-SBM FK matcher, the per-column structural causal model, and the homophily-controlled label overlay as a single multi-threaded pipeline that emits the database directly in rkyv-serialised form, ready for the rustler-based context sampler used during pre-training, with no Python intermediate or pickle round-trip. Two design choices give most of the speed-up: (i) the per-table SCM is laid out as a vectorised computation graph, so MLP propagation and cross-row aggregation are batched across rows of a table rather than executed row-by-row in Python; (ii) the bipartite HSBM is sampled in a pre-allocated buffer with a single pass over the cluster product, avoiding the per-edge Python overhead in the original implementation. End-to-end this brings the per-database generation time from roughly 9090 seconds in the public Python implementation to ∼50​ms\sim\!50\,\text{ms} on a single CPU thread, an approximately 1700×1700\times speed-up at our settings. A 10241024-database corpus, which would take more than a day to produce in the Python pipeline, is generated in well under one minute and re-runs of the corpus during ablations are essentially free.

Appendix H Comprehensive Model Comparison

Here, we show the full results.

Baseline implementation.

For the row-level GNN baselines (RDL-GNN, NBFNet, RelGNN), we use the Relatron framework for hyperparameter tuning, running 1010 HPO trials per task and selecting the best checkpoint by validation performance. RelGT and RT use their original code bases, also with 1010 HPO trials per task and the same validation-based checkpoint selection. For JUICE, we run the original code and add support-side ensembling on top of it. For RDB-PFN, we use the original code together with the fast DFS implementation provided by JUICE to generate the DFS-format features it expects, and follow the default 88-group support ensembling. RT-Plurel uses the official 512512-database, 1616B-token checkpoint released by the authors. For Griffin, we use the original code and pre-trained checkpoint and run their preprocessing pipeline; despite our attempts to optimise the architecture, the inference path remains too slow to be usable on the larger tasks in our suite, and we report only the subset that fits within the compute budget. For KumoRFMv1, we follow the official GitHub example for v1, use Claude Code to draft the PQL queries and few-shot examples for each task, and sweep a small number of hyperparameters per query, primarily the number of sampled neighbours.

Appendix I Agentic Relational ICL for Link-Prediction Tasks

This section sketches one way to extend OpenRFM to link-prediction recommendation, where the relational signal is not directly available as tabular features. Concretely, we evaluate on rel-hm/user-item-purchase (predict the articles a customer purchases in the next 77 days, scored by MAP@1212).

Strategy.

We reframe the task as per-pair binary prediction: each candidate (u,a)(u,a) pair becomes a row whose columns are relational features, and OpenRFM’s standard predictive-task pipeline applies. The pipeline runs in three stages: (i) a coding agent inspects the schema and task description and proposes a task-adapted set of retrieval channels (recency, repeat-purchase, segment trending, weekly cycle, co-purchase, etc.) that produce a candidate pool; (ii) the same agent emits a deterministic featuriser, with a shared time-cutoff helper enforcing leakage-free pre-cutoff reads; (iii) OpenRFM is frozen and conditioned on a single global support set drawn from train + validation rows (built once per evaluation cutoff and reused across all customers), and its calibrated probabilities are blended with the retrieval-priority rank to produce the top-1212 list.

The three numbers fall in the same ballpark, indicating that an unmodified entity-style ICL stack paired with an agent-generated featuriser can reach the regime of dedicated link-prediction baselines without a bespoke recommender architecture.

Example agent-generated features.

Table 14 shows a representative sample of the per-pair features the coding agent emits for rel-hm/user-item-purchase. The full featuriser produces 2727 columns grouped into five blocks; we list two per block as an illustrative demo.
